html:
A port town on the Thu Bồn River in central Vietnam, which in the 17th and 18th centuries was the main foreign trading port of the Nguyễn lords. Its old town of wooden shophouses survives almost whole.

Long before, the area had been a port of Champa. Under the Nguyễn, Hội An, called Faifo by Europeans, held yearly fairs where Japanese, Chinese, Portuguese and Dutch merchants bought silk, sugar, aloeswood and ceramics. Japanese traders on licensed red seal ships had their own quarter, and the famous covered Japanese Bridge is credited to them. When Japan closed its ports in the 1630s, the Japanese community faded, and Chinese settlers, many of them refugees after the fall of the Ming, took the lead. Their assembly halls still line the streets.

The Tây Sơn wars of the 1770s damaged the town. Later the river silted up and Đà Nẵng became the main port, which left Hội An a quiet backwater. That is why it kept its old buildings. UNESCO listed it in 1999.
